201-252 The Role of Subject-Matter Knowledge and Interest in the Processing of Linear and Nonlinear Texts Patricia A
Jetton Texas A&M University Sixty-six studies were reviewed that met several a priori criteria

Specifically, the studies had to be empirical investigations that related to a particular academic domain and that involved connected discourse presented either in traditional written form or on computer
In addition, the studies had to incorporate some measure of both knowledge and interest

The resulting body of literature was first summarized and analyzed in terms of the domains chosen, the subjects selected, the nature of the texts used, the manner in which knowledge and interest were assessed, and the principal outcomes reported
Next, from this analysis, six premises were proposed as guides for future research and practice
Finally, concluding remarks were advanced that ad­ dress the overall significance of text-processing research that interactively considers the domain of knowledge and the interest of the reader

Recent research has brought increasing attention to the importance of subject- matter knowledge in human learning and development (e.g., Chi, Glaser, & Farr, 1988; Glaser, 1984; Glaser, Lesgold, & Lajoie, 1987)
As this research has indicated, it is difficult to overestimate how much individuals' prior knowledge contributes to future learning within a particular field of study

Yet, even more recently, the role of subject-matter knowledge has been juxtaposed with other cognitive and affective variables for the purpose of examining interactive effects (Alexander, 1992; Dochy, 1992; Perkins & Salomon, 1989; Pintrich, 1989; Prawat, 1989)
For those engaged in this interactive, domain-related research, it is not a question of whether existing subject-matter knowledge influences subse­ quent learning

Rather, for these researchers, it is a question of how additional factors in the learner or the learning environment (e.g., personal interest or instructional materials) mediate or mitigate the effects of that knowledge
Two examples may help to illustrate what we mean by interactive, domain- related research

Alexander, Kulikowich, and Jetton action of domain knowledge and general strategy knowledge in academic perfor­ mance
Their purpose was to understand better how these two powerful forces might operate in consonance or dissonance
One of their findings was that strategic processing was more effective and efficient when individuals possessed at least a foundation of domain knowledge
They also posited that the nature of strategy use changed as individuals became more knowledgeable in a domain
In another interactive investigation, Schiefele, Krapp, and Winteler (1992) studied the effects of interest on academic achievement by means of a meta- analysis
Schiefele et al.'s aim was to identify patterns across a body of research that might clarify how motivational factors impact academic learning
One of their conclusions was that gender seems to play a role in this relationship
What they uncovered in the studies they reviewed was a significant difference between males and females with regard to the relationship between interest and academic achievement
Specifically, interest explained 12% of the reported variance for males but only 6% for females
Again, these are just two illustrations of the research that has considered subject-matter knowledge in association with other influential factors in the learner or the learning environment
It is the goal of this review to expand on the aforementioned research and other studies by examining literature that investigates subject-matter knowledge interactively
That is, we will consider subject-matter knowledge in relation to the form of text used in instruction and in conjunction with learner interest

From an educational standpoint, we believe that such a review is significant because it allows one to understand better the way that one's knowledge in a particular field interplays with variables that have been judged as critical to learning, text, and interest

Likewise, from a theoretical standpoint, it is our hope that the premises we derive from this review can serve as guides for future multidimensional studies of subject-matter knowledge, text, and interest

In many ways, we feel, as do others (e.g., Pintrich & Schrauben, 1992; Salomon, Perkins, & Globerson, 1991), that educational research has matured beyond the stage where theory and practice are well informed by studies that investigate single variables in con­ trolled or contrived ways
Specifically, this review of the literature focused on two general types of texts, linear and nonlinear
First, we have been actively engaged in text research for a number of years and are familiar with literature in that realm

Further, we found that many researchers exploring subject-matter knowledge from a complex, interactive perspective used text as a central component in their investigations (e.g., Hidi & Baird, 1986; Hidi, Baird, & Hildyard, 1982; Salomon, Globerson, & Guterman, 1989; Tyler & Voss, 1982; Walker, 1987)

Finally, from the field of science (Yore, 1991) to the domain of social studies (Beck & McKeown, 1988), text remains a principal means by which individuals acquire subject-matter knowledge (Chall & Conard, 1991)
We use the term linear text to designate connected discourse presented in written form where decisions relative to processing are left solely to the reader
Defined in this manner, linear text is text of a more traditional nature—that is, the writings students are apt to encounter in textbooks, journals, and magazines
Nonlinear text is also connected discourse, however; it is discourse accompanied 202 at GEORGE MASON UNIV on June 4, 2016 http://rer.aera.net Downloaded from

This system guides or prompts readers to reaccess or extend the main text through associative computer-based links to other informational screens (see Gillingham, Young, & Kulikowich, in press, for an extensive discussion of the nature of nonlinear text)
One category of nonlinear texts that we will inspect in this review, for example, is hypertext

With the evolution of situated theories of learning that emphasize rich and unique learning environments (e.g., Brown, Collins, & Duguid, 1989; Greeno, 1989; Resnick, Levine, & Teasley, 1991), nonlinear texts, such as hypertext, have gained in popularity

Many of these hypertexts are part of extensive multimedia systems that include not only nonlinear texts but also supporting videos, maps, and commercial movie clips (Christensen, Giamo, & Jones, 1993; Trumbull, Gay, Mazur, 1992)
Therefore, it is important to consider the impact of these more nontraditional texts on the acquisition of subject-matter knowledge (Bolter, 1991b)
As with others (e.g., Pintrich & Schrauben, 1992; Weinstein & McCombs, in press), we acknowledge the influence of noncognitive variables in one's develop­ ment within an academic domain
In deciding how to incorporate the noncogni­ tive (i.e., motivational) dimension to this review of subject-matter knowledge, we decided to concentrate our efforts on the construct of interest

This decision was made, in part, because of the inconsistent findings regarding the relation­ ship between interest and knowledge that have been reported in the literature (Schiefele et al., 1992; Tobias, in press)
In addition, our own research has recently led us to question the role that interest plays within various stages of domain learning (Alexander, in press; Alexander, Jetton, & Kulikowich, 1993)
For the purpose of this review, we defined interest to be both situational and individual (Hidi, 1990; Schiefele, 1991)
By situational interest, we mean the transient attention or emotional response to elements within the text or the context
Individual interest, on the other hand, refers to a more long-term, deep- seated interest in the domain from which that content arises
In the sections that ensue, we first articulate the criteria and the procedures we followed in conducting this review

Next, we summarize and analyze the litera­ ture we identified, and then we forward basic premises about the interrelation­ ship of subject-matter knowledge, interest, and linear and nonlinear text that we hope can guide future endeavors

Finally, we offer concluding remarks that speak to the significance of subject-matter research that attends interactively to learner interest and to the nature of the instructional text used in the learning environment

Method Criteria for Inclusion Our first task in this review was to specify the criteria that would serve as our decision rules for the inclusion or exclusion of particular literature selections and to stipulate the procedure to be followed in locating and summarizing each work
Following extended discussions, we determined that literature would be included in this review if it met four criteria
First, whether quantitative or qualitative in approach, the work had to be empirical

Reviews of the literature, like Hidi's (1990) synthesis on interest, while useful as a source of relevant research, leading 203 at GEORGE MASON UNIV on June 4, 2016 http://rer.aera.net Downloaded from
Alexander, Kulikowich, and Jetton questions, or guiding hypotheses, were not explicitly analyzed in this review

Second, there had to be an academic domain of study that was either specified by the researchers or that we could discern from the given information, such as the descriptions of the experimental materials

Studies, such as Bromley and Mahlios's (1985) investigation of good and poor readers' text-processing strate­ gies, were not included because they did not offer adequate information on the domain from which the text was drawn
Such a problem was rather common in studies in the fields of reading and writing and led to the exclusion of a number of investigations in our initial pool
Third, text had to be a component in the study, and, further, that text had to be connected discourse
Thus, studies that centered on isolated words or sentences were excluded from our review

This criteria resulted in the elimination of only a small number of studies from our initial pool, among them Anderson's (1982) work on selective attention for which the experimental stimulus was a list of unconnected sentences
Although the study had to involve discourse, the text could be presented in either linear or nonlinear form
The comparison of these two forms of text was an important dimension of this review because these forms of discourse were indicative of more and less traditional learning environments

Some recent work by the Cognition and Technology Group at Vanderbilt (1990, 1992) on videodisc environments, while relevant to learning environments, was not summarized because it did not specifically incorporate text as we have defined it in this review
We fre­ quently found literature that addressed either knowledge or interest but rela­ tively little that specifically examined both
In a study by Shirey and Reynolds (1988), for example, there was an investigation of the effects of interest on text learning
However, there was no measure of subject-matter knowledge involved in the study, excluding it from our analysis

Reciprocally, Walker's (1987) excellent investigation on the relative importance of domain-specific knowledge and general aptitude to subject-matter learning could not be analyzed, because it did not include any measure of interest

There were also several cases, partic­ ularly in the domains of mathematics and science, where the researchers investi­ gated participants' knowledge and attitudes but did not include any specific measures, subscales, or items that related directly to interest

Henk and Holmes's (1988) research on the effects of content-related attitudes on comprehension and Schibeci and Riley's (1986) examination of the influence of background and perceptions on students' attitudes and achievement in science were studies eliminated from the review for this reason
Overall, this particular criterion, more than any of the preceding three, resulted in the exclusion of studies in our initial pool from final review
First, we generally restricted our search to the period extending from 1983 to the present because we felt that most pertinent literature would have been reported within the past decade
However, we decided to include any research reported prior to that date if it were frequently cited or if we knew it to be central to our review
Hidi et al.'s (1982) classic study, entitled "That's Important But Is It Interesting

Subject-Matter Knowledge and Interest Two Factors in Text Processing," is an example of a study published before 1983 that we incorporated in our review
Next, we examined a number of on-line retrieval systems, including Psychological Abstracts, Educational Resources Information Center, and Dissertation Abstracts

Key words that were used to identify prospective writings included the term knowledge, or such knowledge- related descriptors as comprehension, recall, achievement, prior knowledge, or learning, and the term interest, or such interest-related descriptors as attitude, affect, intrinsic motivation, and preference

Even though we used related terms, such as attitudes, to search for relevant literature, we included only those writings that fit the operational definitions of subject-matter knowledge and interest we offered at the outset of this review
Along with these database retrieval systems, we physically scanned the vol­ umes of 65 journals from various fields
Again using key words, we perused the title and abstract of each article
If additional information were required to determine the suitability of an article, then the materials section and the description of the variables were also inspected
Finally, using the same process, we examined the contents of books, technical reports, and papers from conferences, such as the American Educa­ tional Research Association

On the basis of this search procedure, we identified an initial pool of over 750 published and nonpublished works that seemed to include some combination of variables of concern in this study (i.e., knowledge, text, and interest)
From this initial pool, 66 studies met the criteria for inclusion we specified earlier
Summary and Critical Analysis To assist us in analyzing the 66 studies identified for this review, we first summarized them with regard to central characteristics

Specifically, as seen in Appendix B, we recorded: • the authors and the year reported, • the domain or domains researched, • the number and type of subjects, • the nature of the text (i.e., whether linear or nonlinear), • a further description of that text (e.g., length and topic), • when knowledge was measured (i.e., pretest or posttest), • how knowledge was assessed, • whether interest was pretested or posttested, • the type of interest measure used, and • the principal outcomes of the research
In examining these basic characteristics, we identified some general trends across the studies
For example, over 75% of the studies meeting our stated criteria have been reported in the last 5 years
This is especially true for the research involving nonlinear text, the vast majority of which has appeared since 1990
In light of the increasing sophistication in domain-related research and the recency of multimedia approaches, such as hypertext, this trend is quite under­ standable

Alexander, Kulikowich, and Jetton Domains Despite the number of domain-related journals we examined, we found that those researchers exploring subject-matter knowledge, in conjunction with text processing, tended to cluster in a relatively few fields
Predominantly, identified studies involved texts drawn from the domains of literature, psychology, social studies, and science
Relevant studies were also located in the domains of mathematics and computer science
It might be argued that this clustering of domains is partly the result of our decision to restrict this review to research involving connected discourse
While this argument cannot be discounted, it is not a sufficient explanation for this overall trend

For one, literature may have been a preferred domain because it is the primary medium by which students learn to read in schools (Purvis, 1981), thus making it particularly appealing to researchers in language and literacy
For another, it seemed that literature was a domain selected by researchers working with both linear and nonlinear text because of its ill-structured nature (Bolter, 1991a)
This ill-structured quality not only allowed for the study of cognitive processing or strategic behavior (e.g., Salomon et al., 1989) but also for what Beeman et al
used to designate the critical analysis of concepts in one domain from the perspective of another domain
For instance, one can analyze the writings of Dickens from the perspective of Victorian literary style or from the social class issues that were operating at that time
A similar interdisciplinary explanation could also be applied to some of the research we reviewed in social studies

By using passages drawn from social studies, however, researchers (e.g., Hidi & Baird, 1988; Wade & Adams, 1990) were not only able to stimulate pluralistic thinking, but they were also able to include an array of topics (e.g., "Easter Island" and "Inventors") likely to interest readers

In addition, those working with social studies texts were able to manipulate certain text variables, such as importance and interestingness of specific information, as well as the overall structure of the text (e.g., narrative, pseudonarratives, and exposition)
These types of manipulations were central to the researchers' questions of how the nature of the text influenced subjects' learning
The frequency of relevant studies from the domain of science appeared to be linked with the current interest in students' misconceptions (e.g., Morrell, 1992)
Some researchers used what Carlsen and Andre (1992) described as conceptual change texts
These texts, which typically included both linear and nonlinear components, were intended to confront common misconceptions in such areas as genetics or electric circuitry
Thus, the text was an important tool for conveying accurate and detailed information about complex concepts that were difficult for students to comprehend accurately
In several of these mathematics studies where computer-based or computer-as­ sisted instruction was utilized, the text was in the form of extended word or story problems
Here, the choice of domain seemed more related to students' interests in the field than to their knowledge base or the nature of text processing

One exception to this observation was the program of research by Ross and colleagues (e.g., Murphy & Ross, 1991; Ross, McCormick, & Krisak, 1986)
In this re­ search, Ross and his colleagues were quite concerned with the nature of the text because they wanted its contents to be closely aligned with students' interests

For exam­ ple, Murphy and Ross (1991) sought to make mathematics more meaningful to students by constructing story problems with themes of personal interest to the students (e.g., animals, sports, and clothing)
First, it appeared as if the choice of psychology was most often a pragmatic decision rather than a theoretically driven one

That is, in these investigations, the researchers may have chosen a content-area of convenience because no explicit or implied explanation was offered as to why this content was considered over any other (Benware & Deci, 1984; Schiefele, 1991, Exp

It might be surmised, however, that, once the decision was made to use college students, the choice of psychology texts was reasonable because the students could read texts that were authentic (i.e., actual chapters in textbooks) or relevant to their college studies

Students were occasionally asked to read and react to written materials that were both highly contrived and rather irrelevant to their academic pursuits (e.g., Garner, Alexander, Gill- ingham, Kulikowich, & Brown, 1991), although this observation applies more to studies using linear than nonlinear text

Subjects Studies employing more traditional text covered the spectrum of school-age subjects, whereas those requiring subjects to manipulate the text via a database system most often studied students of high-school and college age

When database systems were used with younger students (i.e., elementary or middle-school students), these systems were often utilized to promote written composition processes (e.g., Turner & Dipinto, 1992) or to foster cooperative learning strategies (e.g., Signer, 1992)
It is likely that the demands of navigating through the computer-based system, particularly hypertext, is too challenging for youn­ ger learners, restricting the applicability of such programs

Indeed, in one study (Egan, Remde, Landauer, Lochbaum, & Gomez, 1989), the researchers hired experts in statistics so that they could study these experts' interactions with a hypertext system and the search strategies which they employed
(As above, we will make reference to students' navigation through nonlinear text

By naviga­ tion, we are referring to the readers' movement from one segment of text to another or from the text proper to other screens, tools, or options, such as supporting videos, maps, and commercial movie clips.) Further, in relation to the subjects, we were somewhat surprised by the sample sizes

Perhaps because they tended to use computer classes as their source of subjects or because of the ease of data collection, approximately 60% of the nonlinear text studies employed large samples (range: 20-252)
Even more of the linear text studies had large samples (74%), and their range in sample size was comparable (range: 20-540)

Occasionally, gender or ethnic background was referenced (e.g., Anderson, Wilkinson, & Mason, 1991; Kinzie, Sullivan, & Berdel, 1992), but even this information was unavailable for a number of the investigations, particularly those involving older subjects or those summarized in edited volumes (e.g., Wade, 1992)

When we consider that gender has been suggested as a significant factor in the interplay of knowledge and interest (Schiefele et al., 1992), the failure of researchers to consider such information seems problematic
For our purposes, the lack of data was particularly acute in terms of the background knowledge and experiences of the subjects
As we will discuss later, researchers often made assumptions about subjects' relevant knowledge, based on age or grade level, but failed to provide empirical support for those assumptions
Texts It is interesting to note that the linear and nonlinear texts described in these studies varied on a number of attributes
For instance, easily over one third of the traditional texts were expressly written, manipulated, or contrived for the partic­ ular research study; a trend not evidenced with nonlinear texts
Garner, Gill- ingham, and White (1989), for example, structured brief exposition on insects to highlight particular "seductive details" (p
(1991) manipulated a passage on Stephen Hawking to strategically position personally involving content dealing with his battle with a life-threatening illness
With nonlinear text, there was a greater tendency for the researchers to integrate a variety of original, resource texts (e.g., journal articles and scientific papers) with visual and graphic aids

With some exceptions (Anand & Ross, 1987; Morrison, Ross, & Baldwin, 1992), there was much less manipulation or generation of text in these studies, unless that manipulation or generation was done by the subjects, who were free to create a text using a collection of source materials (e.g., Egan et al., 1989)
In addition, the texts used in the computer- based or hypertext investigations were characteristically lengthy—much more so than was typical in the studies using more traditional texts
The length of these nonlinear texts may be another reason why subjects in these studies tended to be older

We were intrigued by the number of researchers who used modified or unmodified excerpts from encyclopedias in their investigations (e.g., Asher, Hymel, & Wigfield, 1978; Baldwin, Peleg-Bruckner, & McClintock, 1985; Wade & Adams, 1990)
Perhaps their decisions to use passages from encyclopedias were based on the accessibility of these reference materials in schools and, thus, students' familiarity with them
Indeed, encyclopedias are ready sources of short exposition on a wide array of topics
Yet, this frequent use of texts from encyclopedias also concerned us for several reasons

Despite their popularity, we are not convinced that entries in encyclopedias are particularly well crafted as text, nor are we sure that these reference materials present a topic in any depth or detail
Therefore, students asked to process passages drawn from encyclopedias may be required to learn from incoherent or unengaging texts that treat a topic in a rather superficial manner
Regrettably, in a number of studies, little information beyond a cursory mention of the text was provided (e.g., Dillon, 1991)

However, in those studies where the researchers purposely wrote or manipulated the text, much more information was typically given as to why that particular topic or passage was chosen or why certain features of the text were judged important

This may have to do with the fact that these researchers, many from the fields of reading or educational psychology, were much more concerned with general text processing than with domain-specific issues
For these individuals, the selection of a domain-related passage was, in essence, a secondary or tertiary issue
The richer text descriptions among these researchers may also be related to the fact that some chose texts to correspond to subjects' reported likings or preferences (e.g., Hidi & Baird, 1988)
Therefore, more elaborate descriptions of the texts were required to substantiate this correspondence
Whether the text was linear or nonlinear in nature, knowledge was in many cases assessed in a post hoc rather than in an a priori fashion (e.g., Wade, 1992)

For the most part, researchers seemed more interested in measur­ ing subjects' comprehension or recall following the processing of text than they were in gauging subjects' preexisting knowledge relative to the selected field or text

As we noted, some researchers (including these authors) assumed that students, as a consequence of their age or their educational level, would possess the general or domain-specific knowledge necessary to process the given content effectively (Alexander, Jetton, Kulikowich, & Woehler, in press; Jetton, Alex­ ander, & White, 1992; Morrell, 1992)

For example, in a recent study, Alexander, Kulikowich, and Schulze (in press-a) found that undergraduates reported almost no knowledge about the standard model in physics and relatively little knowledge about Stephen Hawk­ ing and grand unification
While the researchers expected the reading tasks to be somewhat demanding, they never anticipated the dearth of physics knowledge they encountered among educated students
In the studies that deviated from this general pattern (e.g., Alexander, Kulikowich, & Schulze, in press-a, in press-b; Faircloth, 1984; Schiefele, 1992b, Exp
I; Steele, 1985; Walton, 1982), pretest measures were occasionally adminis­ tered either to control for or to categorize subjects on the basis of their knowl­ edge

In the case of Schiefele's (1992) experiment involving computer-science majors' processing of psychology texts, the goal was to ensure that subjects had little preexisting knowledge of the textual content
By contrast, Alexander, Kulikowich, and Schulze (in press-a) categorized students as low knowledge or high knowledge on the basis of their pretest performance on a domain knowledge test
This knowledge differential proved to be a significant factor in both the students' interest in the content and their recall of the passage information
Prior subject-matter knowledge also proved to be a significant variable in the study by Garner et al
In this study, students' level of domain knowledge militated against the personally involving information included in a passage about Stephen Hawking and the grand unification theory

Further, recent work by Scardamalia and Bereiter (1992) showed that the familiarity of students with the topic of endangered species helped those who did not have text materials on the topic ask more knowledgeable and more interesting questions than students who asked questions on the topic after reading a related text

Alexander, Kulikowich, and Jetton and Doucette (1992) also found that students with high knowledge and interest were better able to predict the questions that their professors would ask
Clearly, a variety of knowledge measures were used, including free recalls, grade-point averages, achievement test scores, short-answer and open-ended questions
However, the most common format for assessing students' knowl­ edge, including both standardized and researcher-generated measures, was via multiple-choice questions

It is likely that ease of scoring was one factor that contributed to the popularity of this measurement format, along with the useful­ ness of multiple-choice items in covering a breadth of subject matter

Further, while most of the measures assessed declarative knowledge, there were some procedural knowledge measures applied, particularly in the computer-based studies (e.g., an assembling task; Dillon, 1991; a figural construction task; Morrison et al., 1992)

We observed that there was an apparent relationship between the domain under study and the preferred knowledge measure, with researchers in science and mathematics often choosing standardized achieve­ ment data in contrast to those in reading and literature who chose structured and unstructured recall measures
Interest Whereas knowledge was most often measured post hoc, interest was often assessed both at the outset of the research and at its conclusion
When measures of interest were taken prior to text processing, they were often done to determine students' preferences for particular topics (e.g
hobos; Hidi et al., 1982) or for a subject-matter area (e.g., meteorology; Gardner, Simmons, & Simpson, 1992)
Such measures of interest are more aligned to what Hidi (1990) labeled individ­ ual interest

By comparison, when researchers had subjects report their interest during or immediately following text processing, they were frequently concerned with aspects within the immediate situation that produced temporary excite­ ment, attention, or interest (Garner & Gillingham, 1992; Sadoski, Goetz, & Fritz, 1993)

Those measurements that were a bit more difficult to classify as either individual or situational interest were those that were associated with interest scales admin­ istered as part of mathematics, science, or computer studies, or with attitude measures containing interest items (e.g., Jegede, Okebukola, & Ajewole, 1991; Morrell, 1992)

In these cases, such items (e.g., "Computer Assisted Instruction [CAI] makes learning interesting") appeared to incorporate aspects of both situational and individual interest, depending on the respondents' interpretation of intent; that is, did the student respond in relation to the task at hand (e.g., the specific computer program) or in terms of a long-term orientation to the content (e.g., computers or computer-based learning in general)

As was the case for knowledge, the variety of measures used to assess interest was extensive, ranging from sentence underlining (e.g., Alexander, Kulikowich, & Schulze, in press-a), to ratings of interestingness (Wade & Adams, 1990), to questions inquiring about subject-matter interests or topic preferences (e.g., Murphy & Ross, 1991)
Whether ratings, surveys, or questionnaires were used to assess interests or preferences, many researchers (e.g., Monroe, 1991) used a Likert-type scale that ranged from 1 to 5 or 1 to 10 points

This approach, which occurred most often in the computer-based studies, resulted in very limited information on subjects' interest in the domain or the experimental task

As we noted, the assessment of interest was sometimes made at a global level in relation to a field of study (e.g., science; Romance & Vitale, 1992), a particu­ lar topic (e.g., inventors; Hidi & Baird, 1988), or the use of technology (e.g., Gardner et al., 1992; Guthrie & McPherson, 1992)

At other times, however, the researchers were concerned with gauging subjects' immediate interest in a particular text selection (e.g., quarks; Alexander, Kulikowich, & Schulze, in press-b) or some segment of that text (e.g., wager between Hawking and Kip Thome; Garner et al., 1991)

It is noteworthy that in several studies where traditional texts were used, particularly the seductive detail research (e.g., Garner et al., 1989; Wade & Adams, 1990), subjects' recall was used as an indicator of interest
(1989) study, for instance, students' recall of specific information from text was contrasted against experts' ratings of interest and importance for those same text segments
Outcomes Five trends with regard to the principal outcomes reported in our 66 studies are especially noteworthy

First, although we made the a priori decision to include both quantitative and qualitative studies, our literature review was composed almost exclusively of quantitative research (i.e., 65 out of 66 studies)

It may well be that the research question we posed regarding the role of subject- matter knowledge and interest in the processing of linear and nonlinear texts is a question most likely considered or analyzed quantitatively
It might also be that, as quantitative researchers ourselves, we have missed rich qualitative sources that speak to this empirical question
Second, and related to the previous issue, researchers overwhelmingly em­ ployed group comparison procedures such as analysis of variance and analysis of covariance to determine their outcomes
Within-subject perspectives among these studies were, with rare exceptions (Alexander et al., 1993; Anderson- Inman & Horney, 1993), forgotten or ignored
(1993) have suggested, this failure to consider within-subject data may overlook some signifi­ cant relationships between knowledge and interest variables that are obscured by group means
Employing within-subject techniques, Anderson-Inman and Horney (1993), for example, were able to identify three prototypic hypertext users based on their comprehension and interest
Indeed, in their discussions of results, some researchers acknowledged their reliance on group comparison procedures and the potential influence this reliance may have had on their reported outcomes
Lanza and Roselli (1991), for example, reported no signifi­ cant differences between hypertext and more structured computer-based in­ struction groups on posttest measures
However, the researchers noted the extreme variability in the hypertext distribution which suggested a masked differential in the way subjects navigated through that system

Third, in the computer-based or hypertext studies that we examined, there were few significant gains in knowledge reported, although there were some 211 at GEORGE MASON UNIV on June 4, 2016 http://rer.aera.net Downloaded from
Alexander, Kulikowich, and Jetton significant effects for interest and attitudes (e.g., Schare, Dunn, Clark, Soled, & Gilman, 1991; van der Berg & Watt, 1991)

We attribute this trend to the fact that, in these nonlinear text studies, subjects were not only operating in complex domains (e.g., genetics or statistics) but that they were also required to navigate through very complex computer-based systems
In other words, the compound­ ing effect of a complex domain within a complex instructional system resulted in minimal effects on knowledge acquisition (e.g., McGrath, 1992)
It is encourag­ ing, however, that subjects' interest in the domain or their attitudes toward the computer-based system were often positively influenced
Fourth, as others have (Schiefele et al., 1992; Tobias, in press), we noted the inconsistent findings for the relationship of knowledge and interest variables in the studies we reviewed

As we will discuss further in the section that follows, this inconsistency could be the result of any number of factors, particularly the varied and sometimes questionable way that these two constructs were measured
However, what surprised us even more, and what serves as the basis for this final observation, is the realization that so few studies specifically considered the interaction of knowledge and interest
While we were able to locate a number of investigations in which both variables were present, their interrelatedness was rarely embraced as an important or central issue by the researchers
